name: Satin bonnet / durag

card.summary: The silky head wrap that holds waves and protects hair overnight; a cultural staple with no clinical trials.
card.aka: Durag, do-rag, wave cap, silk bonnet
card.note: Overly tight tying may strain edges (per Grokipedia).

quick.overview:
A durag or satin bonnet is a smooth cloth cap worn to protect hair, keep moisture in and hold wave patterns in place, especially overnight. It originated in African American grooming culture.

It is central to wave-brushing routines. No clinical studies were found on its hair-health effects.
quick.mechanism: The smooth fabric reduces friction against bedding and the snug fit compresses hair so it lies flat. Sources describe this as holding the style rather than changing hair growth.
quick.risks: Grokipedia says overly tight tying may cause edge breakage. Durags have also drawn dress-code bans in sports and schools.

lead: A durag (also do-rag) is a close-fitting cloth head covering tied around the head to protect hair; a wave cap serves a similar purpose, and a satin bonnet is a related soft, smooth-lined cap worn for the same protective reasons. The durag originated in the African American community and is typically made of silk, satin, polyester or cotton.[1]

People wear them to encourage waves, curls or locs to develop, retain moisture, reduce breakage and keep wave patterns and braids from shifting during sleep, so the hair looks neater, shinier and more defined the next day.[1][2] In wave-brushing and looksmaxxing circles the durag is part of a standard 360 waves routine.[3]

The garment also has a notable cultural history, including dress-code bans in sport and schools and a 2020 appearance on a British Vogue cover.[1] No clinical trials of its effect on hair were found; descriptions of how it works come from encyclopedic and community sources.

chain: Smooth cap worn over brushed or styled hair
Reduces friction and holds moisture and pattern in place
Waves, curls or braids look more defined and polished
angle.text: People tie a durag or put on a satin bonnet after brushing and moisturising, usually overnight, so waves or styles stay set. The smooth fabric also reduces friction against bedding.

infobox: Hair covering (cloth cap tied at the nape)
Silk, satin, polyester, cotton, velvet, mesh[1][2]
Overnight and daytime protection, wave training

paras: Durags have a main panel with long ties that cross at the back and knot at the nape or forehead.[2] Silk is described as prized for smoothness, while satin and polyester are common lower-cost options, velvet versions are marketed for extra compression, and mesh versions serve warm conditions.[2] Wave caps are a stretch-fit alternative.[1] Grokipedia lists tying styles such as the classic back tie, front tie, no-knot tuck and ski-mask style, while noting its content is AI-generated.[2]

The Oxford English Dictionary cites a 1964 pamphlet as the first printed use of the word, and Merriam-Webster dates it to 1968.[1] The Black Pride movement of the 1960s and 1970s made the durag a fashion statement, and William J. Dowdy is reported to have mass-produced the first modern tie-down durag in 1979.[1] Rappers including Jay-Z, Nelly and 50 Cent popularised it in the 1990s, and Rihanna's 2020 British Vogue cover is cited as a milestone for the garment as fashion.[1] Songs naming it include Frank Zappa and George Duke's 1974 'Uncle Remus' and Thundercat's 2020 'Dragonball Durag'.[1]

In 1995 the NFL considered banning durags, with an executive linking them to crime, but took no action; in 2001 owners voted 30 to 1 to ban most headwear under helmets, and critics raised concerns of racial bias while some players argued durags helped prevent hair loss.[1] The NBA's 2005 dress code banned durags on court and on team business, and in 2019 John Muir High School in Pasadena banned them, prompting a student walkout.[1]

For waves, the usual description is to brush and moisturise the hair and then put on a durag or wave cap to hold moisture and compress the hair.[3] Grokipedia states that durags do not promote hair growth, and that overly tight tying may cause tension and edge breakage; both statements come from an AI-generated source.[2] On T Nation, one member says he lines everything touching his head with satin or silk, using an inexpensive pillow cover and a bonnet, and does not consider expensive versions necessary.[5]

Wikipedia's traction alopecia article lists tight headwear worn snugly for years among the causes of pulling-related hair loss, which presents mainly at the temples and hairline, and treatment centers on reducing chronic tension.[4] Grokipedia likewise notes that overly tight tying may cause edge breakage.[2]

lore.intro: Durags and satin bonnets come up mainly in wave-brushing routines and in general hair-care talk about silk lining.[3][5]

claims.claim: A durag overnight keeps waves set and protects hair from friction
claims.believers: Wave-routine descriptions say the cap holds moisture and compresses hair in place, and a T Nation member lines headwear and pillows with satin or silk.[3][5]
claims.experts: No clinical trials were found; descriptive sources say it reduces friction but does not promote hair growth.[2]

claims.claim: Tying a durag very tight gives better waves
claims.believers: Compression is described as how the cap trains the hair to lie flat.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists tight headwear among causes of traction alopecia.[4]
